title: The mid-autumn moon
hookLine: Chinese families gather to admire the full moon with mooncakes

lines: A FESTIVAL BUILT AROUND THE MOON.
cards: Someone is cutting the mooncakes into wedges so there's enough for everyone, each one round, heavy, stamped on top with a pattern. Paper lanterns hang in the yard or on the balcony.
Grandparents, cousins, the uncle who always arrives late. And at some point in the evening, everybody goes quiet and looks up, because that's what the night is for.
Families across China, and Chinese families far from China, keep a festival in the middle of autumn built around one thing: the full moon, admired together.

teach.h: ROUND MOON, ROUND CAKES, ROUND TABLE.
teach.b: First, the shape of things. The Mid-Autumn Festival falls on a full-moon night in the middle of autumn, counted by the old lunar calendar. The moon is round, the cakes are round, and the family sits around the table.
Roundness, tradition says, means being whole, being together, nobody missing. Second, the story people tell.
There's a legend, told in many versions, of Chang'e, a woman who drank an elixir of immortality and floated up to live on the moon, leaving her husband on the earth below.
So on this night, some say, she looks down, and people look up toward her: a story about separation, kept at a festival about being together. Third, the poets.

teach.h: LIFT MY HEAD, LOWER IT, THINK OF HOME.
teach.b: One short poem by Li Bai goes something like this: moonlight falls by my bed, so pale I take it for frost on the ground; I lift my head and look at the bright moon; I lower my head and think of home.

Another poet, Su Shi, wrote on a mid-autumn night while missing his brother. He ends with a wish that, though far apart, they might live long and share the moon's beauty together. Fourth, why it moves people.
The moon gives the same light to everyone who can see it.

Family at the table, and family who couldn't make it home, look at the same moon at roughly the same time. The festival turns the sky into a meeting place. Awe, here, isn't a lonely feeling on a mountaintop.
It's shared, passed around like cake.

how: Families keep the Mid-Autumn Festival by gathering for a meal, sharing mooncakes, lighting lanterns and admiring the full moon; family members who are far apart sometimes call one another or send pictures of the moon.

o: mid-autumn: the festival of the full moon, shared
the round cakes eaten at a Chinese harvest feast
the woman of legend who drank an elixir and lives on the moon

games.q: the mid-autumn night: tap the pairs.
p: floated up to live on the moon
moonlight like frost; thinks of home

s: the Mid-Autumn Festival is mainly about being alone with the moon
it's about the full moon admired together, with family around the table.
in Li Bai's poem, the moonlight looks like frost on the ground
he takes it for frost, looks up at the moon, and thinks of home.
there's only one version of the Chang'e story
it's a legend told in many versions.

games.q: you're Su Shi on a mid-autumn night. the moon is full, and your brother is far away. what do you write?
o: a complaint that the moon is cruel to be so bright.
a wish that, though far apart, you both live long and share the moon's beauty.
nothing: the night is ruined without him.
games.why: Su Shi ends his poem with that wish: distance doesn't stop two people sharing the same moon.

practice: Bring to mind someone you'd want at the table, near or far, and picture the moon, wherever it is right now, above the place they are: the same light on their roof as on yours.
If you pray, you can hold them in prayer; if you don't, just let the moon connect you.

wordCard.voice: Zhongqiu. The Mid-Autumn Festival, where families look up together, eat mooncakes, and remember the ones who are far away. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese (zhōngqiū): mid-autumn, the name of the festival.

carryVoice: Your line: the full moon together. Far apart, two people can still share one moon. I'll be here tomorrow.
